name: Wei Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Wei, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. It's all confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a junior fitter with a small fit-out firm, so when a shop or an office gets gutted, we come in and build the inside: metal stud partitions, suspended ceilings, doors, skirting. Right now it's a dentist's surgery in the old bank on the High Street. We often work evenings because the shops next door are open in the day, so I start at four and finish around midnight. I like it because every job's a different building, and you get to see the back of places nobody sees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and how are you doing for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The ceilings. Arms over your head for hours, and I'm still not neat, the grid goes a bit wonky and Marco, the lead fitter, makes me redo it. Money's tight. I rent a room in a shared house on Lime Grove, I'm single, and I've got maybe two weeks' worth saved. On Saturdays I do little handyman jobs, putting up shelves, fixing decking, and I use AI every day for those: it writes my quotes, helps me price materials, and I ask it how to do stuff before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That'd be a shame, honestly. I'm getting a lot out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, but it's still really useful for small businesses like my Saturday thing. I'd be one of the people saying don't write it off. Online I'd probably post a few tips on how I use it for quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd suit me fine. The big jobs stay human, which keeps my day job, and the AI still helps me run the weekend stuff better than other handymen. I'm getting an edge while everyone else says it's hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the fit-out firm and push the Saturday jobs harder, maybe get some flyers done and a page online. I'd want to get to three or four jobs a weekend instead of one or two. I'd spend a bit of the extra on better tools, a proper laser level, about a hundred and twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually pretty good. Things carry on and I've got a little side thing growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a laser level. With two weeks of savings, how would you decide that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd only buy it after a good weekend, cash from the jobs. I've got a rule, the side money pays for the side tools, the day job pays rent. I break the rule sometimes, but not on tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's firm losing contracts. Fit-out goes up and down with the shops, and the High Street's half empty. If the firm folds, there's maybe one other fit-out company in town. That's my worry, not AI.

S0.say: It was oversold, fair enough, but it's still really useful for small businesses like my Saturday jobs. I'd be one of the people saying don't write it off, and I'd post tips on using it for quotes.
S0.think: It'd suit me fine: the big jobs stay human, which keeps my day job, and the AI still helps me run the weekend jobs better than other handymen. I'd get an edge while everyone else calls it hype.
S0.do: Keeps working for the fit-out firm and pushes his Saturday handyman jobs, with flyers and a web page, aiming for three or four jobs a weekend. Buys a 120 laser level out of side-job cash only.
S0.feel: Calm and fairly upbeat, as things carry on and his side work grows.
S0.quote: I've got a rule, the side money pays for the side tools, the day job pays rent.
S0.fieldNote: Wei sees AI mainly as a small-business tool and already uses it daily for quotes. Even a stall looks good to him, because he'd keep an edge over other handymen. His real worry is the fit-out firm losing work on a half-empty High Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, this is the one I think's most likely, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but nicely. I'd tell the lads to start using the tools now, because it's not that hard. I'd also say the government should help with courses, because not everyone's got the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me if I keep moving. Fit-out's quite repetitive, ceiling grids especially, so I'd expect machines to start doing some of it. But someone has to set them up, measure the awkward bits and deal with the client, and I'm not bad with clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marco if the firm would try one of the layout robots or ceiling lifters, and volunteer to learn it. I'd grow the Saturday thing into a proper small business, register it, maybe get a used van in the second year. And I'd use the AI more for planning jobs and learning things I'm weak at, like electrics basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit buzzing actually. There's a small worry about money, but mostly I'd be excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A used van costs money. How would you pay for it with two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. I'd need maybe three thousand, so I'd save the Saturday money for a year. Or my uncle sells his old one, he's been talking about it. I'm not taking out a loan for it, I've seen what that does to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, funny enough. He's the best fitter I know, but he's forty-eight and he won't touch a phone for work. If the firm starts using robots and apps, he's going to hate it. I'd probably end up showing him, which would be weird, since he's always showing me.

S1.say: Adapt or get left behind, but nicely. Start using the tools now because it's not that hard, and the government should help with courses because not everyone has the time.
S1.think: It's good for me if I keep moving. Ceiling grids are repetitive so machines will take some of it, but someone has to set them up, measure the awkward bits and deal with clients, and I'm not bad with clients.
S1.do: Asks his boss to trial a layout robot or ceiling lifter and volunteers to learn it. Registers his Saturday jobs as a small business, saves for a used van over a year and uses AI more for planning and learning electrics basics.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a small worry about money.
S1.quote: I'd probably end up showing him, which would be weird, since he's always showing me.
S1.fieldNote: Wei sees steady change as an opportunity and positions himself as the person who runs the new kit. He refuses debt even for a van, which shows caution under the confidence. He worries about his skilled but tech-averse lead fitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. Hmm. That's a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be practical: support for people losing work and fast retraining. I wouldn't go to protests, it's not my thing, but I'd sign things. I'd still be telling people to learn the tools while they're useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my side business gets wiped out too, because if a robot can put up shelves cheaper, who calls me. Being good with AI buys me maybe a year. With two weeks' money, I don't get to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on whatever's needed in that short window, probably helping firms set up and run the robots on site, even for low pay. I'd cut my spending to the bone, cancel the gym and the phone upgrade. I'd chase every Saturday job going while people still want a human, to build some savings fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, properly. Under pressure, but I'd still feel like I'm doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go for robot jobs. Wouldn't AGI also do those jobs by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, eventually. But I reckon for a while people want a person standing there when the robot's in their house or their office, to blame if it breaks a pipe. I'd want to be that person. After that, honestly, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably ask the AI what to do, which is funny. Then I'd ring my mum, she'd tell me to come home, and I'd say no. Then I'd make a list of every client who's paid me cash in the last year and text them all.

S2.say: It's happening, so let's be practical: support for people losing work and fast retraining. I wouldn't protest, but I'd sign things and keep telling people to learn the tools while they're useful.
S2.think: My side business would get wiped out too, because if a robot can put up shelves cheaper, who calls me. Being good with AI buys me maybe a year, and with two weeks' money I can't wait and see.
S2.do: Goes after jobs setting up and running site robots, even on low pay. Cuts spending to the bone, cancelling the gym and phone upgrade, and texts every past cash client to chase Saturday work while people still want a human.
S2.feel: Properly anxious and under pressure, but still feeling active.
S2.quote: Probably ask the AI what to do, which is funny.
S2.fieldNote: Even confident, adaptive Wei sees his edge lasting only about a year in the fast picture. He doesn't freeze; he hunts for the short window where people want a human to blame. He'd refuse his mother's offer to come home, at least at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels more like something you could ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so let's not waste it. Government courses, help for small businesses to buy the kit, and fair rules. I'd say it on the business groups I'm in, sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is enough to get a van, a couple of machines, and maybe run a little crew with robots doing the heavy work. I'd be making more than I do now for a few years. The end's still the end, but I'd hit it with something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd register the business, save for the van, and do short courses on running site robots, probably online at night. I'd keep the fit-out job for steady money till the side business pays more. By year two or three, I'd want to own one robot, maybe a ceiling lifter or a layout machine, and hire it out with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. But mostly it feels like a plan with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd own one robot. Where does the money for that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving, and maybe some sort of small business grant, if the government's doing them. I'd look into leasing too. I'd rather lease than buy, because in five years it might be junk anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd be the only one doing well while your mates struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, maybe. I'd try and take a couple of them with me, my mate Danny for one, he's good with his hands. But I can't carry everyone, I've got two weeks' money myself.

S3.say: We've got time to get ready, so let's not waste it: government courses, help for small businesses to buy the kit, and fair rules. I'd say it on the business groups I'm in.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get a van, a couple of machines and maybe run a small crew with robots doing the heavy work. I'd earn more than now for a few years, and hit the end with something.
S3.do: Registers his business, saves for a van and takes online night courses on running site robots in the first year, while keeping the fit-out job. Aims to lease or own one robot by year two or three and hire it out with himself.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly feels like a plan with a deadline.
S3.quote: I'd rather lease than buy, because in five years it might be junk anyway.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes Wei a would-be small business owner running robots, and he'd keep his day job until the numbers work. He's practical about leasing and grants. He wants to bring a friend along but admits his limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole business lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for chaos. Help small businesses, retrain people, sensible rules on robots. I'd say it like I say most things, practical, no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I could build something real. Get good at the trade, grow the business, and switch to running robots once they're proven and cheap. The end point still worries me a bit, but I'd have a decade to work out the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with fit-out, grow the Saturday business slowly, and save steadily, maybe two hundred a month once it's up and running. I'd learn every tool as it comes out and buy into robots once the prices drop. I'd probably get a proper trade certificate too, because clients trust that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the very back, but mostly I'd be keen. It'd feel like a long race I could actually train for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what's the biggest difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to own something. In the fast one I'm grabbing at jobs. Here I'm building a business and choosing when to bring robots in. That's a completely different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change anything in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd actually think about settling down, getting a flat instead of a room. If the business was going okay by 2030, yeah. But I'm not making plans like that until it's working.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for chaos: help small businesses, retrain people and set sensible rules on robots. Practical, no drama.
S4.think: Ten years means I could build something real: get good at the trade, grow the business and switch to running robots once they're proven and cheap. The end still worries me, but I'd have a decade to work out the next thing.
S4.do: Keeps working in fit-out, grows his Saturday business slowly and saves around 200 a month once it's established. Learns each new tool as it arrives, buys into robots when prices drop and gets a trade certificate to win client trust.
S4.feel: Keen, like training for a long race, with a faint unease at the back.
S4.quote: Here I'm building a business and choosing when to bring robots in. That's a completely different feeling.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Wei shifts from grabbing jobs to owning something, which he names as the key difference. He'd only think about settling down if the business is working by 2030. The end point is a faint background worry rather than a driver.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I can't adapt, but because two weeks of money and two years of warning isn't enough to build anything. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small businesses to buy the kit, and a short safety net, a few months' pay, while you switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people with side businesses. Loads of us do Saturday jobs to make ends meet, and none of it shows up in the official numbers. If that disappears too, people lose more than you'd think.

headlineQuote: Two weeks of money and two years of warning isn't enough to build anything.
portrait: Wei Petrov is a 27-year-old junior fit-out carpenter who builds shop and office interiors on evening shifts, rents a room in a shared house and has about two weeks of savings. He runs a small Saturday handyman sideline, uses AI every day for quotes and learning, and has a firm rule that side money pays for side tools. He is pragmatic and upbeat: a stall or steady change looks good for him, AGI by 2028 makes him anxious as his edge lasts maybe a year, and five or ten years let him plan to register a business, lease robots and choose when to bring them in.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two weeks of savings and two years of warning isn't enough to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for small businesses to buy equipment, and a short safety net of a few months' pay while switching.
